extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (real analysis / discrete math / elementary set theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions to undergraduate-level exercises on inequalities, continuity/monotonicity, bijections, countability, and cardinality; demonstrates standard proof techniques and explicit constructions of injections/bijections. Useful as a model for writing rigorous proofs in these topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-negativity of squares to derive inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use that the square of a real number is non-negative (and of a non-zero real number is positive) to produce inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: '(2x − 1)^2 ⩾ 0' expanded to '4x^2 − 4x + 1 ⩾ 0' and rearranged to obtain '1 ⩾ 4x(1 − x)'. Also used as 'Recall that the square of any non-zero real number is positive' to get strict inequalities like (x − y)^2 > 0. This is a standard pattern: form a square term and expand/compare to obtain the desired inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide by positive quantity without changing inequality direction
rubrics_metrics.description: When both sides of an inequality are divided by a positive quantity, the sign of the inequality is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: 'Since x, y > 0, hence xy > 0 and we may divide both sides by xy without changing the sign of the inequality' used to go from x^2 + y^2 > 2xy to x/y + y/x > 2. Always verify the divisor is positive before dividing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (assume negation and derive impossibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the claim and derive a logical contradiction, often reducing to an impossible statement (e.g., a nonnegative square being strictly negative or equalities that contradict distinctness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: assuming x,y>0 and x≠y but x/y + y/x ⩽ 2 leads to (x−y)^2 ⩽ 0, contradicting non-negativity of squares; assuming equality of two different cardinalities and deriving contradiction. Typical structure: assume contrary, manipulate algebraically, use prior facts (squares ≥0, IVT, etc.) to obtain contradiction, conclude original claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove bijectivity by showing injective and surjective separately
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a function is a bijection, establish injectivity (f(x)=f(y) ⇒ x=y) and surjectivity (for each y in codomain construct x with f(x)=y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous examples: explicit proofs for functions such as f(n)=n−1 (N→N∪{0}), f(n)=3^{n−1} (N→{1,3,3^2,...}), and f(m,n)=2^{m−1}(2n−1) (N×N→N). The proofs follow the standard pattern: injective: assume equality of images and deduce equality of preimages; surjective: given target, produce an explicit preimage (often by inversion or number-theoretic decomposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit arithmetic encodings to build bijections
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct bijections by encoding tuples or structured objects into integers (or vice versa) using prime powers, parity, or factorization patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(m,n)=2^{m−1}(2n−1) to encode N×N into N via powers of 2 and odd factors; mapping sequences to decimal expansions 0.b1b2... for bijection with [0,1). Use uniqueness of prime factorization or parity/odd-even decomposition to argue injectivity and surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) to contradict injectivity of non-monotone continuous maps
rubrics_metrics.description: If a continuous function is not strictly monotone, find x1<x2<x3 with f(x1) ≤ f(x2) and f(x3) ≤ f(x2) (or the reverse). Use IVT to produce a point x0 ≠ another point with same f-value, contradicting injectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text demonstration: For a continuous bijection f:R→R, assuming it increases then decreases leads via IVT to distinct x0 and x3 with f(x0)=f(x3), contradicting injectivity. This yields the criterion: a continuous bijection on R must be strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis splitting (equality vs inequality; sign or ordering cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break proofs into cases (e.g., x = y vs x ≠ y, d>0 vs d<0, a+b ≤1 vs a+b>1) and handle each separately, combining results at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: e.g., proving x/y + y/x ⩾ 2 handles x=y and x≠y separately; solving quadratic-derived surjectivity distinguishes d=0 and d≠0 then further subdivides by sign. Be explicit about why the cases cover all possibilities and how they combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct bijections between intervals and R via standard monotone maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Use known monotone bijections (exponential, reciprocal, shifts) and compose them to map between R, (0,∞), (1,∞), and (0,1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: g(x)=e^x maps R→(0,∞); f(x)=2^x+1 maps R→(1,∞); reciprocal maps (1,∞)→(0,1) by x↦1/x. Compose these to obtain explicit bijections R↔(0,1). Provide inverses (log, reciprocals, shifts) to verify bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal expansion/representation carefulness (avoid non-unique representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using decimal expansions to construct bijections, choose a canonical representation (avoid expansions ending with infinitely many 9s) to ensure uniqueness and injectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when mapping (0,1)×(0,1) to (0,1) by interleaving digits, the text specifies choosing the decimal representation that does not end with repeating nines so that the interleaving is injective. Also be aware some targets are not in image due to representation choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal enumeration (Cantor-style) to enumerate countable unions or tables
rubrics_metrics.description: List elements of an array/table by diagonal sweeps to enumerate the union of countably many countable sets, taking care with empty cells and duplicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text shows constructing a table with rows listing elements of each denumerable set and enumerating by diagonals to get a bijection N→⋃_n A_n. Ensure each diagonal sweep reaches a non-empty cell (first column non-empty) so enumeration covers all elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show set is countable by injection into a known countable set
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a set S is countable, construct an injective map from S into a countable set (often N^k or N) or construct a surjection from N onto S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For Fn (finite n-subsets of N) define injection into N^n by ordering elements ascending; N^n is countable so Fn is countable. Similarly, show union of countably many finite/countable sets is countable via injections/surjections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein (CSB) application for cardinality equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A|, apply CSB theorem to conclude |A| = |B|. Use injections both directions or construct them using known bijections/compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text uses CSB to deduce equalities of cardinalities and shows equivalence of a statement about chains of inequalities implying equalities to CSB. Also use CSB to combine injections to show two sets are equinumerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct power-set bijection induced by base bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a bijection f:A→B, define F:𝒫(A)→𝒫(B) by F(C)={f(a):a∈C} to obtain a bijection between power sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text (12.7.15) constructs F from f and proves injectivity and surjectivity of F by using inverse f^{-1} and properties of f. This is the standard method to lift bijections to power sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show uncountability by finding an uncountable subset or bijection with [0,1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a set is uncountable by constructing a bijection with an already uncountable set (e.g., [0,1) or 𝒫(N)) or by exhibiting a subset that is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: map sequences of digits (excluding those ending in infinitely many 9s) bijectively to [0,1) to show uncountability; map binary sequences to 𝒫(N) via indices of 1s (f((c1,c2,...))={k:ck=1}) to conclude uncountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble bijections on disjoint pieces to build global bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: If A∩C=∅ and there are bijections f:A→B and g:C→D with B∩D=∅, define F on A∪C piecewise by F(x)=f(x) for x∈A and F(x)=g(x) for x∈C to get a bijection A∪C→B∪D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text provides this construction and checks injectivity and surjectivity case-by-case; ensure domains/codomains are disjoint or handle overlaps carefully so definition is well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use minimal-index selection in unions/partitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When decomposing elements of a union of sets (or working with partitions), pick the minimal index n for which the element belongs to demonstrate membership in a chosen disjoint subcollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In proving ⋃_n A_n = ⋃_n B_n with B_n = A_n \ ⋃_{k<n} A_k, choose N = min{n : x∈A_n} to show x∈B_N, thereby proving the decomposition and disjointness of the B_n.
